strengths: The paper addresses a relevant high-dimensional classification setting and clearly motivates estimating a whitening transformation under an exact spiked-covariance model.

The entrywise eigenspace analysis and resulting infinity-norm bound for the whitened mean difference are potentially useful contributions under the stated fixed-rank, divergent-spike, incoherence, and fixed-sparsity assumptions.
The method is conceptually simple, and the manuscript provides detailed algorithms, proof appendices, several baselines, a sensitivity experiment, and two real-data examples.
The presentation is generally organized enough for researchers in high-dimensional statistics to identify the intended contribution and its relationship to sparse discriminant analysis.
weaknesses: Necessary: The QDA extension is mathematically invalid. Equation (5.5) drops all coordinates outside the support of the whitened means, but sparsity of W_i mu_i does not eliminate the covariance-dependent quadratic terms in those coordinates when Sigma_1 differs from Sigma_2. For example, sparse whitened means together with different isotropic bulk variances satisfy the model yet allow the omitted p-dimensional variance signal to drive the Bayes error toward zero. Consequently Theorem 6 and the prominently advertised QDA Bayes-optimality claim are false without substantially stronger assumptions and a new proof.

Necessary: The claimed extension to general sub-Gaussian elliptical distributions is also unsupported. For a non-Gaussian radial density h, the likelihood ratio contains log h(q_1)-log h(q_2), which is not the Gaussian LDA score in general, particularly with unequal class priors. Concentration of the parameter estimates only establishes convergence to the Fisher rule; it does not make that rule Bayes optimal. The claim must be restricted to conditions under which the Bayes boundary is actually linear or replaced by a weaker target.

Necessary: The reported oracle simulation results conflict with the stated data-generating models. Under balanced classes in Model 2, the stated 20-by-20 equicorrelation block and ten unit mean shifts imply Bayes errors of approximately 5.28%, 3.62%, 1.96%, 0.59%, and 0.02% as rho goes from 0.5 to 0.9, whereas Table 3 reports roughly 5.3% throughout. Table 1 likewise reports 0.19% at rho=0.8 instead of approximately 0.022%, with several entries apparently duplicated from rho=0.7. The simulations therefore need to be audited, rerun, and made reproducible before their evidence can be trusted.

Necessary: The main LDA claim is broader than the proved result. The abstract asserts a growing-sparsity condition s sqrt(log(p)/n) -> 0, but Assumption 2 fixes s and imposes a constant beta-min condition, and the manuscript explicitly leaves growing s unproved. Moreover, the proof of Theorem 3 invokes log(n)log(p)=o(n), ends with joint score convergence in probability, and does not establish the stated almost-sure convergence of conditional risk under merely log(p)=o(n). The statement, proof, and abstract must be reconciled.

Necessary: Adaptivity to the unknown spike rank is not established. The assertion that the largest sample bulk eigenvalue is O(sigma^2) is false when p/n diverges; for isotropic noise, nonzero sample eigenvalues can scale as p/n. The experiments instead use a 90%-explained-variance heuristic, which may retain many bulk components and is not covered by the fixed-d theory. Either analyze the implemented selector or remove the adaptivity guarantee.

Necessary: The whitening estimator is ambiguously defined. Lambda contains spike increments, so population spike eigenvalues are lambda_k+sigma^2, while hat Lambda is described as containing the full leading sample eigenvalues and is then used as (hat Lambda+hat sigma^2 I)^(-1/2), apparently adding the bulk variance twice. This must be corrected consistently across the algorithm, theory, and implementation.

Necessary: Claims about selecting fewer features require narrowing. A selected whitened coordinate is generally a dense combination of all original variables, so the reported model sizes are not comparable to counts of raw variables selected by sparse LDA methods and do not reduce measurement requirements. The real-data evidence also consists of only one small fixed test split per dataset, with insufficient preprocessing and reproducibility detail.

Optional: Runtime experiments, released code, repeated or nested validation on the biological datasets, and a careful editorial pass over notation and typographical errors would improve usability, but these do not resolve the theorem-level and numerical-validity problems above.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/tmlr_2025plus--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-pneba_ep/call-09c6c250c07148dc97f100bb40001c5d/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} studies an interesting alternative to sparse-discriminant-direction methods: sparsity after symmetric whitening under a dense, strong-spike covariance model. This is relevant to researchers working on high-dimensional discriminant analysis and factor models.

The proposed procedure is explicit, computationally motivated, and accompanied by entrywise eigenspace, whitened-contrast, and support-recovery analyses. The distinction between raw discriminative variables and whitened coordinates is explained carefully.

The empirical section compares several established baselines, reports both errors and representation sizes over 200 simulation replications, includes two real gene-expression datasets, and offers a sensitivity experiment for the number of spikes.
The paper is generally well organized, places its assumptions relative to prior sparse-LDA work, and provides substantial proof details.
weaknesses: Necessary: The QDA extension is not valid as stated. Equation (5.5) is not equivalent to the Bayes QDA rule: the set A0, defined through supports of Σ_i^{-1/2}μ_i, captures mean information but not covariance-only discrimination. For example, sparse whitened means supported on one coordinate together with σ1≠σ2 satisfy the intended structure, yet the other p−1 bulk coordinates are informative and can drive Bayes error to zero while (5.5) discards them. Theorem 6 therefore establishes, at most, consistency for a restricted score—not convergence to Bayes risk. This prominent claim must be removed or rebuilt using assumptions controlling the quadratic covariance-difference term; Assumption 9 also needs Θ(p)-type spike separation rather than merely O(p) for the invoked eigenspace argument.

Necessary: The core LDA Bayes-consistency theorem lacks a required prior-sampling condition. The setup treats n1 and n2 as class-conditioned sample sizes, while Assumption 3 only requires n1/n2=Θ(1). Consequently, the assertion in (8.46) that log(n1/n2) converges to log(π1/(1−π1)) does not follow from a strong law. With balanced training data and an unequal test prior, the limiting classifier is not Bayes optimal. The theorem must assume n1/n→π1, use a consistent external prior estimate, or state a balanced-prior result.

Necessary: The proof of Theorem 3 ultimately invokes log(n)log(p)=o(n), which is stronger than the stated log(p)=o(n), and the transition from a joint test-score bound to almost-sure convergence of the conditional risk is not fully justified. The assumptions, convergence mode, and proof need to be aligned.

Necessary: The whitening estimator is internally inconsistent. Hat Λ is defined as containing the largest sample-covariance eigenvalues, so adding hat σ² again in hat D=(hat Λ+hat σ²I)^{-1/2} double-counts the bulk variance. This also makes identity (8.31) false under the given definitions. The estimator should use hat Λ^{-1/2}, or hat Λ must be consistently redefined as estimated spike strengths, followed by revised bounds.

Necessary: The reported oracle simulations conflict with the stated models. Under Model 2, the squared Mahalanobis distance is [10−100ρ/(1+19ρ)]/(1−ρ), so the equal-prior oracle error should fall from about 5.28% at ρ=0.5 to 0.02% at ρ=0.9; Table 3 instead remains near 5.4%. Likewise, Model 1 at ρ=0.8 implies approximately 0.022% oracle error, not 0.19% as reported. The simulation code and all affected conclusions require an audit.

Necessary: Section 7.3 overstates the elliptical-distribution extension. For unequal priors and a general radial density h, the Bayes comparison is π1h(q1) versus π2h(q2), which is not generally the Gaussian linear threshold unless log h is affine. Sub-Gaussian tails do not repair this. The result should be restricted appropriately, such as to Gaussian generators or suitable equal-prior conditions.

Optional: The empirical claims would be more convincing with repeated real-data resampling and uncertainty estimates, experiments for the multiclass and QDA extensions, runtime measurements, and a clearer qualification that selected whitened coordinates are dense combinations of raw variables. Model-size comparisons are otherwise difficult to interpret, especially because the proposed method's search is capped at 30 coordinates.

strengths: The paper studies a well-motivated problem with an identifiable audience: classification under strong latent-factor covariance structure, using symmetric whitening followed by sparse screening. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/tmlr_2025plus--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-o2vqk99b/call-a9112c0f06854492a7a4cea637922f29/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

For the common-covariance setting, the use of two-to-infinity eigenspace perturbation bounds is technically interesting. The coordinatewise error analysis, support-recovery strategy, and detailed proof decomposition provide a plausible and useful result under fixed sparsity, linearly diverging spikes, and incoherent eigenvectors.

The experiments include 200-replicate simulations with standard deviations, an oracle, several established baselines, multiple covariance structures, a sensitivity experiment, and two real datasets. Within this scope, the method often attains competitive error while selecting a substantially smaller whitened representation.

The manuscript is generally well organized, clearly distinguishes sparsity of the whitened and raw discriminant directions, and provides extensive related-work discussion and supplementary derivations.
weaknesses: Necessary: The QDA extension contains a fundamental error. Equation (5.5) drops all coordinates outside A0, where A0 is defined only from the supports of Wi μi. In general, the omitted term ||[W1(Z−μ1)]A0c||²−||[W2(Z−μ2)]A0c||² is nonzero and carries covariance-discrimination information. Assumptions 5–10 do not make it cancel, so the reduced rule is not equivalent to the Bayes QDA rule and Theorem 6 does not establish convergence to Bayes error. Assumption 9 also gives only an O(p) upper bound on spikes, with no lower eigengap sufficient for the invoked eigenspace consistency. The QDA claim must be removed or rebuilt with appropriate covariance-signal assumptions and proof.

Necessary: The main LDA claims exceed the proved regime. Assumption 2 combines a fixed beta-min condition with bounded ||ζ||, which itself forces s to remain bounded; it therefore does not support the abstract's growing-sparsity condition s√(log p/n)→0. Moreover, the proof of Theorem 3 explicitly requires log n·log p=o(n) and concludes convergence in probability, whereas the theorem states only log p=o(n) and claims almost-sure risk convergence. The abstract, theorem, and proof need mutually consistent conditions and convergence modes.

Necessary: Adaptivity to the number of spikes is not established. The formal theory assumes known fixed d, while the accompanying argument incorrectly states that post-spike sample eigenvalues are O(σ²); for p≫n, even isotropic-noise sample eigenvalues are generally of order p/n. The implemented 90%-variance heuristic is different from the proposed ratio rule and is validated only in one specially chosen sensitivity configuration. Either provide a correct selection result aligned with the implementation or narrow the adaptivity claim.

Necessary: The asserted extension to general sub-Gaussian elliptical distributions is not valid as written. For a non-Gaussian radial density and unequal priors, comparing π1h(q1) with π2h(q2) does not generally yield the linear Fisher boundary in Equation (1.1); covariance concentration alone cannot establish Bayes optimality. This claim requires substantially stronger distributional/prior conditions or should be withdrawn.

Optional: The empirical conclusions would be more convincing with scaling experiments over n and p, tests of the multiclass/QDA/elliptical extensions, uncertainty over repeated real-data splits, and actual runtime measurements for the claimed computational advantage. Releasing the implementation and fully specifying all tuning grids would also improve reproducibility; a careful copyedit would remove numerous notation and grammar errors.

strengths: The manuscript studies a relevant problem for researchers interested in high-dimensional classification, PCA, factor models, and covariance estimation, with a clear motivation for screening after whitening. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/tmlr_2025plus--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-viwka5b_/call-ba33863dc9474c3cbbdc025af9d51da3/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The entrywise eigenspace analysis is potentially useful: Theorems 1–2 give explicit two-to-infinity and coordinatewise rates under clearly stated spiked-covariance, incoherence, and sparsity assumptions.

The numerical section compares several relevant sparse-discriminant methods, reports variability and representation size, and includes dense, block, random-factor, sensitivity, and gene-expression examples.
The main exposition is generally well organized. Algorithms, assumptions, and connections to prior high-dimensional LDA literature are presented clearly enough for the intended audience.
weaknesses: Necessary: The QDA Bayes-optimality claim is invalid as written. Equation (5.5) replaces the full QDA statistic by coordinates in A0 = supp(W1μ1) ∪ supp(W2μ2), but sparse whitened means do not imply that Wi(Z−μi) vanishes outside A0. Covariance differences can carry discriminative information in every omitted coordinate. Theorem 6 only proves consistency for this restricted statistic, not equivalence to the Bayes rule. Moreover, Assumption 9 gives only λik = O(p), whereas the preceding whitening analysis requires spikes and eigengaps of order Θ(p). The QDA claim must be withdrawn or supported by substantially stronger structural assumptions and a complete proof.

Necessary: The elliptical-distribution extension is overclaimed. For a general common radial density h and unequal priors, the Bayes rule compares log h(q1)−log h(q2) with a prior-dependent threshold; it is not generally Fisher's linear rule unless log h is affine in q, as in the Gaussian case. Equal priors recover a linear comparison under suitable monotonicity. Sections 7.3 and the multiclass extension therefore require narrower conditions or a new argument.

Necessary: Theorem 3 does not match its proof. Assumption 3 states log p = o(n), while the proof ultimately requires log n·log p = o(n). It establishes convergence in probability of a random test score but does not adequately derive the claimed almost-sure convergence of the conditional risk. In addition, n1/n2 = Θ(1) does not imply log(n1/n2) → log(π1/(1−π1)); the result needs n1/n → π1 or known priors.

Necessary: The advertised adaptivity is not established for the implemented procedure. Theory assumes fixed d and fixed sparsity and uses a deterministic hard threshold, whereas experiments select d by a 90%-variance heuristic and s by cross-validation. The claim that the first sample bulk eigenvalue is O(σ²) is false when p≫n, where noise eigenvalues scale as p/n. An implementable, justified estimator is needed, and any growing-sparsity claim should be proved or removed.

Necessary: The whitening estimator is ambiguously or incorrectly defined. If Λ̂ contains the largest eigenvalues of the sample covariance, as explicitly stated, then D̂=(Λ̂+σ̂²I)^(−1/2) counts the bulk variance twice. Either Λ̂ must denote estimated spike strengths after subtracting σ̂², or D̂ should use the sample eigenvalues directly.

Necessary: The numerical evidence contains reproducibility problems. For Model 1, the analytic oracle errors at ρ = 0.5,0.6,0.7,0.8,0.9 are approximately 1.314%, 0.649%, 0.206%, 0.022%, and 0.000034%; Table 1 instead repeats 0.19% at ρ=0.8. Several ρ=0.7 and ρ=0.8 entries are exactly duplicated across Tables 1–2. The prose also describes AdaLDA regularization as increasing accuracy when Table 5 shows larger errors, and claims the proposed method has the highest accuracy where some baselines are better. The simulations should be regenerated and accompanied by code, seeds, and preprocessing details.

Necessary clarification: A selected whitened coordinate is generally a dense linear combination of all p raw variables. Thus the reported model-size comparison with methods selecting raw variables is not like-for-like, and the approach does not reduce measurement requirements. Likewise, the whitening map is full-rank rather than a projection onto the leading PCs. Claims about feature selection, parsimony, and PCA dimension reduction should be reframed as selection of transformed dimensions.

Optional: Stronger evidence would include scaling experiments for support recovery and Bayes-risk convergence, broader sensitivity analysis for d, runtime measurements, repeated real-data splits, and experiments for the multiclass, QDA, and elliptical extensions if those claims are retained. These are secondary to correcting the mathematical and numerical issues above. The Gaussian equal-covariance LDA core appears plausibly salvageable, which motivates leaning reject rather than outright reject.

Please evaluate the paper critically using the journal's acceptance criteria and give an overall recommendation according to the scale below.

Then assess whether some members of the intended research audience could learn something of interest and whether the writing communicates those findings clearly enough to understand and use them.

Do not impose a conference-style significance threshold or require a new method or state-of-the-art performance as a condition of acceptance. Distinguish the basic publication criteria from exceptional-impact certifications. Explain necessary changes separately from optional improvements, using the supplied manuscript without assuming a rebuttal or revisions that are not present.

Assign Overall Assessment (OA) using only: 1, 2, 3, or 4.
These numbers are an experimental ordinal encoding of TMLR's textual reviewer recommendations, not an official TMLR numerical score. They do not define equal distances between recommendations.

Rating scale:
1 = reject
The current work fails a required acceptance criterion in a substantive way.

2 = leaning reject
Important concerns about a required criterion remain unresolved, although the work has a plausible path toward satisfying it.

3 = leaning accept
The evidence generally supports both acceptance criteria, with limited reservations that should be stated precisely.

4 = accept
The claims are adequately supported, the findings have an identifiable interested audience, and the paper communicates them clearly enough for that audience.

Output Format

strengths: The problem is well motivated and relevant to researchers studying high-dimensional classification, factor models, and structured covariance estimation. The manuscript is reasonably self-contained and organized. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/tmlr_2025plus--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-r4t9htbj/call-87c9b62d5301474289454db5b9c1533b/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The shared-covariance Gaussian core is conceptually appealing: estimating a structured whitening map and using two-to-infinity perturbation bounds provides a natural route to coordinatewise control and support recovery.

The proposed classifier is simple, and the paper supplies explicit algorithms, comparisons with several established high-dimensional discriminant methods, 200-replicate simulations, a sensitivity experiment, and two real-data examples.
The work could provide an interesting result for an identifiable audience if its claims were restricted to the setting actually established and the main proofs were repaired.
weaknesses: Necessary: The headline QDA result is invalid under the stated assumptions. Equation (5.5) drops every coordinate outside A0, but when Sigma1 differs from Sigma2, the omitted terms ||W1 Z||^2-||W2 Z||^2 generally contain covariance-discrimination information even where both whitened means vanish. Thus (5.5) is not equivalent to the Bayes QDA rule, and Theorem 6 cannot establish convergence to the full Bayes error. The cited consistency of the fitted threshold also does not by itself apply to this different estimated score.

Necessary: The main LDA claim is broader than its theorem. The abstract gives a growing-s condition, whereas Assumption 2 fixes s0, imposes a constant beta-min condition, and bounds the whitened means; Remark 1 leaves growing sparsity unproved. Moreover, the proof of Theorem 3 invokes log(n) log(p)=o(n), which is stronger than the stated log(p)=o(n), and convergence in probability of a random test score does not establish the claimed almost-sure convergence of conditional risk without an additional argument.

Necessary: The prior-probability argument is incomplete. Training is introduced as two class-conditional samples with sizes satisfying only n1/n2=Theta(1), yet the classifier substitutes log(n1/n2) for the test-population prior and the proof asserts convergence to log(pi1/(1-pi1)) by a strong law. This requires an unstated random-label sampling assumption or the explicit condition n1/n2 -> pi1/(1-pi1).

Necessary: The covariance estimator is internally inconsistent. The paper defines hat Lambda as the leading sample-covariance eigenvalues, which already estimate lambda_k+sigma^2, but then uses (hat Lambda+hat sigma^2 I)^(-1/2), apparently adding the bulk variance twice. In addition, the claim that post-spike sample eigenvalues are O(sigma^2) is false when p/n -> infinity; an isotropic bulk has leading sample eigenvalues of order sigma^2 p/n. Consequently, the claimed adaptive estimator of d and its proof are not currently valid or implementable as written.

Necessary: The elliptical extension is overstated. For a general common radial density and unequal class priors, the likelihood-ratio boundary is not generally Fisher's linear boundary; Gaussian exponential structure or additional restrictions such as equal priors are needed. The multiclass extension also inherits the unstated prior-frequency assumption.

Necessary: The empirical evidence is poorly aligned with the theory. Models 1 and 3 have dense whitened directions, Model 2 does not have the required exact equal-bulk/strong-spike structure, and the sensitivity model uses a highly localized eigenvector that violates bounded coherence. Thus no principal experiment tests the joint assumptions of the theorem. The QDA and multiclass claims receive no experiments.

Necessary: Several empirical claims need correction or qualification. The cap s<=30 partly predetermines the reported parsimony in dense models; Table 1 does not show uniformly highest accuracy; the text calls the large deterioration from AdaLDA to AdaLDA(reg) a minimal improvement; and multiple results for rho=0.7 and rho=0.8 are exactly duplicated across Tables 1, 2, 10, and 11, requiring verification or explanation.

Necessary: A selected whitened coordinate is generally a dense function of all p raw variables, so its count is not commensurate with the number of raw features selected by competing methods and does not reduce measurement requirements. Claims of selecting fewer features should be replaced by the narrower claim of using a lower-dimensional transformed representation.

strengths: The paper addresses an identifiable and useful problem: classification when covariance has strong, dense latent factors and conventional sparse-covariance assumptions are unsuitable. The PCA-based low-rank whitening viewpoint should interest researchers in high-dimensional classification. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/tmlr_2025plus--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-2oxkfgot/call-c43d95f7aee14b3d852bf9ce711ef012/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The central LDA analysis follows a coherent technical program: an entrywise eigenspace perturbation bound, uniform estimation of the whitened mean difference, exact support recovery under a beta-min condition, and convergence toward Bayes risk. The assumptions are strong but mostly explicit.

The empirical section is reasonably broad for the core LDA method: it uses 200-replicate simulations under three covariance constructions, several established baselines, cross-validated tuning, selected-dimension reporting, a sensitivity experiment for the spike rank, and two real gene-expression datasets.
The manuscript is well organized, relates the method carefully to sparse LDA and prior PCA-based classifiers, and communicates the main algorithm and intuition clearly enough to be useful.
weaknesses: Necessary: the QDA extension is not valid as written. Equation (5.5) drops all coordinates outside A0, the support of the whitened means, but heterogeneous covariances can carry discriminative information on those coordinates; the omitted quadratic terms do not generally cancel. Thus Theorem 6 only studies convergence to a truncated population score, not to the Bayes QDA score. Assumption 9 also permits weak spikes through an O(p), rather than a separating Theta(p), condition, and the proposed neighborhood for kappa has the opposite sign for the empirical log-prior term. The QDA Bayes-optimality claim must be removed or supported under substantially stronger structural conditions and a complete risk argument.

Necessary: the elliptical-distribution extension overclaims Bayes optimality. For a general radial density h and unequal priors, the likelihood-ratio boundary is not Fisher's linear rule; sub-Gaussian tails ensure concentration but do not make LDA Bayes optimal. The result must be restricted, for example to Gaussian radial form or an appropriately stated equal-prior/common-generator setting, or reformulated relative to the best linear rule.

Necessary: several central LDA claims exceed the proved result. Assumption 2 fixes the support size and imposes a constant minimum signal, whereas the abstract claims a growing-s result under s sqrt(log(p)/n) tending to zero. Moreover, the proof of Theorem 3 invokes log(n)log(p)=o(n), which is not implied by the stated log(p)=o(n), and joint convergence of a test score is asserted to yield almost-sure convergence of conditional risk without the required boundary-continuity and summability argument. These statements and assumptions need to be reconciled.

Necessary: the covariance estimator is internally inconsistent. The manuscript defines hat Lambda as the leading sample eigenvalues, which already estimate lambda_k+sigma squared, but then uses (hat Lambda+hat sigma squared I)^{-1/2}, effectively adding the bulk variance twice; related identities in the proof rely on incompatible conventions. Likewise, the rank-adaptation discussion incorrectly states that non-spike sample eigenvalues remain O(sigma squared) when p is much larger than n, and its asymptotic Omega(log p) rule is not operational. The algorithm, notation, proofs, and practical 90%-variance heuristic need a single consistent treatment.

The empirical evidence supports competitiveness only in the reported settings. Two of the main simulations deliberately violate the theorem's sparsity assumptions, the rank sensitivity study covers one favorable configuration, and there are no experiments for the multiclass, QDA, or elliptical claims. The real-data evidence consists of two small fixed test sets. Broad robustness and extension claims should therefore be narrowed or supported with additional experiments.

The reported 'model size' counts whitened coordinates, each generally depending on all raw inputs, whereas baselines select raw variables. This is a valid representation-dimension comparison but does not establish raw-feature or biomarker parsimony; that distinction should be made explicit. Optional improvements include releasing code and preprocessing details, reporting runtime and memory for the computational claims, varying n, p, spike strength, and sparsity, and correcting the numerous typographical and grammatical errors.

strengths: The paper addresses an identifiable problem of interest to researchers in high-dimensional statistics. Distinguishing sparsity of the whitened mean difference from sparsity of the raw discriminant direction is useful and motivates a genuinely different covariance regime.
The core Gaussian LDA analysis uses entrywise eigenspace perturbation to target support recovery, with explicit assumptions and a substantial proof appendix.
The proposed procedure is conceptually simple, and the manuscript relates PCA, whitening, and sparse discriminant analysis to relevant prior work clearly.

The empirical section includes multiple covariance structures, 200 Monte Carlo replicates, oracle and modern baselines, a sensitivity experiment, and two real datasets. The reported LDA results are often competitive.
The manuscript is well organized at a high level, with readable algorithms and tables, and should be understandable to its intended audience.
weaknesses: Necessary: The headline QDA result is mathematically unsupported. Equation (5.5) is not equivalent to the Bayes QDA rule: sparsity of Wi mui does not make the quadratic covariance terms outside A0 vanish. Coordinates with zero whitened means can still discriminate through Sigma1 versus Sigma2. Consequently Algorithm 4 and Theorem 6 cannot generally be Bayes optimal. The proposed center for the threshold search also has the opposite sign on the estimated log-prior term from kappa in Equation (5.3). This extension must be removed or rederived under substantially stronger conditions.

Necessary: Theorem 3 is not established under its stated assumptions. The classifier substitutes log(n1/n2) for the prior, but Assumption 3 only requires n1/n2=Theta(1); Equation (8.46) additionally requires n1/n to converge to pi1. For example, balanced training data with pi1=0.9 would not approach the Bayes rule. Moreover, the proof invokes log(n)log(p)=o(n), which is stronger than the stated log(p)=o(n), and concludes only joint score convergence in probability rather than the claimed almost-sure convergence of the conditional risk.

Necessary: The whitening estimator is defined inconsistently. Hat Lambda is explicitly called the matrix of leading sample-covariance eigenvalues, yet hat D=(hat Lambda+hat sigma squared I)^(-1/2) adds the bulk eigenvalue again. The proof instead treats hat Lambda as an estimate of spike strengths. Related trace identities are likewise incompatible with the definition in Assumption 1. The algorithm, proof, and experiments must use one correct definition and the numerical results should then be verified.

Necessary: The abstract suggests a growing-sparsity guarantee through s sqrt(log(p)/n) tending to zero, whereas the theorem assumes uniformly bounded support and a constant beta-min condition. Those assumptions, together with bounded norm of zeta, are incompatible with arbitrary growing s. The claim should be narrowed or a valid growing-s theory supplied.

Necessary: The claimed extension to general sub-Gaussian elliptical distributions is too broad. With unequal class priors, Fisher's linear rule is not generally Bayes optimal for an arbitrary radial density; the Gaussian log-density structure is what produces the stated constant prior threshold. Appropriate restrictions, such as equal priors or a suitable radial family, are needed.

Necessary: The numerical evidence needs auditing. Tables 1 and 2 contain exactly repeated results for rho=0.70 and rho=0.80 across several methods, which strongly suggests duplication or an experimental/reporting error. Reproducible code and seeds are not supplied. In addition, the proposed method and CAT-LDA are capped at 30 selected coordinates while several competitors are unrestricted, making part of the parsimony advantage imposed by design. The two real-data conclusions rely on single, very small test splits, and none of the QDA, multiclass, or elliptical extensions is evaluated.

Necessary: The practical choice retaining 90 percent of sample variance can select many noise components in the equicorrelation experiments, conflicting with the fixed-d theory. The sensitivity analysis considers only d=1,2,3 and therefore does not validate the implemented selector; selected d values and broader sensitivity and runtime results are needed.

Optional: Clarify that the whitening map is full-rank and each selected whitened coordinate can depend on all raw variables. Thus model sizes are not directly comparable to raw-feature selectors and the method does not necessarily reduce measurement requirements. Numerous notation and proofreading errors should also be corrected.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant high-dimensional classification problem and gives a reasonably intuitive whitening-and-screening construction for covariance matrices with strong low-rank structure.

The core LDA analysis identifies explicit structural assumptions and makes potentially useful use of entrywise eigenspace perturbation bounds; this could interest researchers working on discriminant analysis and factor models.
The empirical section includes several covariance structures, 200 Monte Carlo replications, multiple sparse-LDA baselines, and reports both error and selected-coordinate counts.
Algorithms and proof sketches are presented in enough detail to expose the main ideas and, notwithstanding numerous presentation errors, the central LDA proposal is understandable.
weaknesses: Necessary: The QDA extension is mathematically invalid as stated. Equation (5.5) is not equivalent to the Bayes QDA rule: sparsity of Wi mui only restricts the linear mean terms, whereas the quadratic term z^T(Sigma1^{-1}-Sigma2^{-1})z generally depends on every coordinate. Covariance differences outside A0 therefore cannot be discarded. Consequently, Theorem 6 and the abstract's QDA Bayes-optimality claim are unsupported and require removal or a fundamentally different set of assumptions and proof.

Necessary: The main LDA Bayes-consistency theorem uses log(n1/n2) as the prior term, but Assumption 3 only requires n1/n2=Theta(1). The proof incorrectly invokes a strong law to conclude n1/n2 tends to pi1/(1-pi1), even though the class-specific sample sizes are presented as fixed. Equal training sample sizes with an unequal test prior give an immediate counterexample. A prior-consistency assumption or a separately estimated/known test prior is required; the multiclass result has the same problem.

Necessary: Theorem 3 claims almost-sure risk convergence under log p=o(n), but its proof obtains only convergence in probability of a single-test-point score and explicitly uses the stronger condition log n log p=o(n). It does not establish convergence of the conditional risk claimed in Equation (3.9). Moreover, the abstract advertises growing sparsity satisfying s sqrt(log p/n) to zero, while Assumption 2 fixes s and the paper explicitly leaves growing-s arguments to the reader.

Necessary: The whitening estimator is internally inconsistent. Lambda-hat is defined as containing the full leading eigenvalues of Sigma-hat and is used that way in the bulk estimator (2.8), yet (2.7)/(3.3) adds sigma-hat squared to those eigenvalues again. Parts of the proof instead treat Lambda-hat as estimating excess spikes. The algorithm, implementation, and rate analysis cannot all correspond to the definitions given.

Necessary: Further extension claims also lack support. Assumption 9 gives only lambda_ik=O(p), which supplies no lower bound or eigengap needed by the preceding perturbation analysis. Consistency of the data-fitted QDA threshold is asserted via results derived under different structural conditions. Likewise, for general elliptical densities and unequal priors, a monotone radial generator does not make the stated Gaussian LDA rule Bayes-optimal; equal priors or substantially stronger restrictions on the generator are needed.

Necessary: The experiments do not evaluate QDA, multiclass classification, or elliptical data despite the associated claims. Three synthetic designs and two old, single-split gene-expression datasets support only a narrow empirical statement about the listed baselines, not general 'state-of-the-art' competitiveness or a substantial computational advantage; no runtime evidence is supplied. Sensitivity to d is tested at only one parameter setting even though underestimating d there changes error from about 0.55% to 24.19%.

Necessary: Counts of retained whitened coordinates are compared with counts of selected raw variables and interpreted as model parsimony. A whitened coordinate is generally a dense combination requiring all p original measurements, so these quantities do not establish comparable feature selection, acquisition cost, or interpretability. Claims should be limited to dimension within the transformed representation.

Optional: The manuscript needs extensive copy-editing and notation checking, including duplicated sample sets in (3.7), inconsistent uses of 'Condition' and 'Assumption,' malformed equation references, grammatical errors, and suspiciously identical entries across several columns of Tables 1 and 2. Releasing code and seeds would also make the numerical evidence auditable.

strengths: The equal-covariance Gaussian problem is relevant to researchers in high-dimensional discriminant analysis, and the distinction between sparsity of the raw discriminant direction and sparsity after whitening is useful.
The proposed PCA-assisted covariance estimator and screening rule are intuitive, computationally simple, and accompanied by detailed algorithms.

The entrywise eigenspace analysis is technically interesting and, after the issues below are resolved, could provide a valuable route to support recovery and Bayes-risk consistency under strong spiked-covariance assumptions.
The empirical section compares several established baselines over 200 Monte Carlo repetitions, reports both error and representation size, and includes two real gene-expression datasets.
The manuscript is largely self-contained and clearly organized, with assumptions, tuning procedures, sensitivity analysis, and proofs collected in sufficient detail to permit scrutiny.
weaknesses: Necessary: The advertised QDA extension is incorrect as written. Equation (5.5) discards coordinates outside A0, defined from the supports of the whitened means, but unequal covariances can contain discriminating information in those coordinates. For example, A0 may contain only coordinate 1 while differing bulk variances make coordinates 2 through p informative. Nothing in Assumptions 5–10 makes the omitted quadratic terms cancel. This invalidates Algorithm 4's claimed reduction and Theorem 6's Bayes-consistency conclusion; the QDA claims must be removed or rebuilt under substantially stronger conditions.

Necessary: The whitening estimator is internally inconsistent. The manuscript defines Λ-hat as the actual leading eigenvalues of the sample covariance, yet uses (Λ-hat + σ-hat² I)^(-1/2), apparently adding the bulk variance twice. Correspondingly, the algebra leading to Eq. (8.31) drops σ²−σ-hat² terms and does not follow from the stated eigendecompositions. The estimator's definition, implementation, and affected proofs must be reconciled.

Necessary: The main consistency claim exceeds what is proved. The abstract allows growing sparsity through s sqrt(log(p)/n)→0, whereas Assumption 2 fixes s0 and explicitly leaves growing sparsity to the reader. Moreover, Theorem 3 claims almost-sure risk convergence under log(p)=o(n), while its proof explicitly obtains convergence in probability and invokes the stronger condition log(n)log(p)=o(n). The theorem, abstract, and multiclass extension require corrected modes of convergence and growth conditions or additional proof.

Necessary: The elliptical-distribution extension is too broad. With unequal priors, a common monotone radial density h does not generally yield the linear Gaussian likelihood-ratio boundary in Eq. (1.1); that conclusion holds under additional restrictions such as equal priors or the Gaussian exponential radial form. Concentration of the parameter estimates alone therefore does not establish Bayes optimality for the stated class.

Necessary: Adaptivity to the spike count d is not convincingly established. The theory assumes known d, the proposed eigenvalue-ratio criterion is expressed using non-operational asymptotic notation, and experiments instead use a 90%-variance heuristic without a general guarantee. The sensitivity study itself shows severe failure when d is underestimated. This claim should be narrowed or supported by a specified, analyzed, and evaluated estimator of d.

Necessary: Claims about selecting fewer features should consistently say “whitened coordinates” or “transformed representation.” Because each selected coordinate can be a dense combination of all raw variables, the reported model size does not imply fewer measured variables, raw-feature sparsity, or comparable interpretability to competing sparse classifiers.

Optional: None of the principal simulations cleanly realizes all theorem assumptions—Models 1 and 3 have dense whitened directions, while Model 2 and the sensitivity construction violate aspects of the divergent-spike or incoherence structure. A scaling experiment satisfying all assumptions and measuring support recovery and excess Bayes risk would connect the theory to the evidence. Releasing implementation code, reporting runtime, and performing a careful copyedit would also improve reproducibility and presentation.

strengths: The equal-covariance LDA problem is well motivated, and the combination of a strong spiked-covariance model, incoherent eigenvectors, and sparsity after symmetric whitening offers an interesting alternative to assumptions of sparse precision matrices or discriminant directions.

Using two-to-infinity perturbation bounds to control the estimated whitener and support recovery is technically interesting and potentially useful to researchers studying high-dimensional factor models.
The manuscript gives explicit algorithms and assumptions, compares several established baselines, reports Monte Carlo variability, and includes two real-data examples plus a sensitivity experiment.

The exposition is largely self-contained and sufficiently organized for the intended audience to identify the proposed idea and claimed results. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/tmlr_2025plus--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-uwsnb0ju/call-2abf74a6e3d649e3bc549081a9bd6aa3/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: Necessary: The QDA extension is mathematically invalid. Equation (5.5) is not equivalent to the Bayes QDA rule: sparsity of Wi mu_i does not make the quadratic covariance terms outside A0 cancel. For example, if sigma_1 differs from sigma_2, every omitted bulk coordinate carries covariance information. Consequently Algorithm 4 and Theorem 6 do not establish Bayes optimality; this headline claim must be removed or replaced by assumptions and analysis controlling the precision-matrix difference.

Necessary: The claimed extension to general sub-Gaussian elliptical distributions is false for arbitrary class priors. For a generic radial density h, the likelihood ratio h(q1)/h(q2) is not a function only of q1-q2, so the Fisher rule with a log-prior offset is generally not Bayes. The claim requires substantial restriction, such as Gaussian radial form or appropriately qualified equal-prior settings.

Necessary: Several gaps remain in the core LDA theory. Theorem 3 assumes log p=o(n), but its proof requires log n log p=o(n); the proof establishes score convergence in probability while claiming almost-sure convergence of conditional risk; and convergence of log(n1/n2) to the population-prior ratio is used without an explicit sampling assumption linking training counts to pi_1.

Necessary: The whitening estimator is internally inconsistent. The paper defines hat Lambda as the leading sample eigenvalues, then adds hat sigma squared again in hat D. This conflicts with the population parameterization and with the algebra used in Equation (8.31). Equation (8.25) also has the wrong sign on its projector-difference term. These are not merely presentational issues because they enter the proof of the main entrywise bound.

Necessary: The adaptive choice of d is not justified as claimed. In the p much greater than n regime, non-spike sample eigenvalues are generally of order p/n rather than O(sigma squared), and an asymptotic condition written as Omega(log p) is not an implementable selector. The experiments instead use a 90%-variance heuristic, which can retain many noise components and is only tested against misspecification by one component.

Necessary: The numerical evidence contains a concrete inconsistency. Under Model 1 at rho=0.8, the stated parameters imply an oracle error of approximately 0.022%, but Table 1 reports 0.19%, exactly duplicating the rho=0.7 entry; several proposed-method and baseline entries are likewise duplicated across those columns. This requires corrected experiments and auditable code before the empirical claims are credible.

Necessary: The reported model sizes are not comparable. Selecting s coordinates after a dense whitening transformation still requires all raw features and generally produces a dense raw-space discriminant direction, whereas competing methods' support sizes count directly selected measurements. Thus the claims of feature parsimony and substantially lower-dimensional operation need to be reframed and supported by runtime, memory, or acquisition-cost measurements.

Necessary: Experiments do not test the central asymptotic setting, support recovery, multiclass method, QDA method, or elliptical extension. The two small fixed real-data test sets provide little uncertainty information, while the simulation tuning procedures differ from those analyzed theoretically.

Optional: The manuscript would benefit from systematic copyediting and notation checking; it contains many grammatical errors, inconsistent symbols and equation references, and avoidable pagination such as the nearly empty page containing only Table 12.

strengths: The paper addresses an identifiable problem of interest: high-dimensional classification with dense spiked covariance structure and sparsity only after symmetric whitening. This perspective is meaningfully different from assuming a sparse covariance, precision matrix, or raw discriminant direction. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/tmlr_2025plus--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-5ex1dmpz/call-681f79a8931142e8996961aef0d2de89/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

For the common-covariance Gaussian setting, using row-wise eigenspace perturbation to control the estimated whitened direction in infinity norm is a promising technical approach. The resulting connection among whitening, support recovery, and Bayes consistency could be useful to researchers in high-dimensional statistics.

The numerical study includes 200-replicate simulations, several covariance structures, oracle results, multiple established baselines, cross-validation, model-size summaries, two gene-expression datasets, and a sensitivity experiment for the number of spikes.
The manuscript is broadly well organized: the algorithms and structural assumptions are stated explicitly, related work is discussed at length, and proofs are supplied in the appendix.
weaknesses: Necessary: The QDA extension is incorrect as written. Equation (5.5) replaces the full quadratic norms in the Bayes rule by coordinates in A0, where A0 is defined only through the supports of W_i mu_i. Covariance differences generally contribute discriminative quadratic terms outside A0—particularly when the explicitly permitted bulk variances differ—so (5.5) is not equivalent to (5.3). The proof of Theorem 6 establishes convergence only to this restricted score and never connects it to the true Bayes score or risk. Assumption 8 does not repair this gap, and Assumption 9 provides only an O(p), rather than a separating lower bound, on spike sizes. The QDA claim requires a substantially different sparsity condition and proof, or should be removed.

Necessary: The principal LDA Bayes-consistency theorem lacks an assumption connecting training class proportions to the deployment prior. Algorithm 1 uses log(n1/n2), while Assumption 3 only states n1/n2=Theta(1) and the initial setup uses class-stratified samples. Thus equation (8.46) does not follow from the strong law. Balanced training with pi1 unequal to 1/2 gives an immediate counterexample. The theorem must assume n1/n converges to pi1 or use an appropriate prior estimate; the same issue affects the multiclass result.

Necessary: The whitening estimator is internally inconsistent. The manuscript defines hat Lambda as containing the largest sample covariance eigenvalues, which already estimate lambda_k+sigma^2, but then sets hat D=(hat Lambda+hat sigma^2 I)^(-1/2), thereby adding the bulk variance twice. This also makes the algebraic identity in (8.31) false as stated. The estimator must be corrected or hat Lambda redefined, followed by an audit of the theoretical rates and experiments.

Necessary: The advertised sparsity and convergence scope exceeds what is proved. The abstract claims consistency under s sqrt(log(p)/n) tending to zero, whereas Assumption 2 fixes s0 by a constant M and imposes a constant beta-min condition and a bounded signal norm, conditions that do not support the stated growing-s claim. Moreover, the proof of Theorem 3 invokes log(n)log(p)=o(n), rather than merely log(p)=o(n), and concludes with joint convergence in probability of a score rather than the claimed almost-sure convergence of conditional risk. These claims should be narrowed or supplied with complete arguments.

Necessary: Adaptivity to the number of spikes is not established. The claim that the largest non-spiked sample eigenvalue is O(sigma^2) is false when p/n diverges; even isotropic noise has a leading sample eigenvalue on the order of sigma^2(1+sqrt(p/n))^2. Consequently, the stated Omega(p) eigenvalue-ratio argument does not follow. The experiments instead use a 90%-variance heuristic, whose only sensitivity study covers one configuration and shows severe failure under underestimation.

Necessary: The extension to arbitrary sub-Gaussian elliptical distributions overstates Bayes optimality. With unequal priors and a non-Gaussian radial density h, the likelihood-ratio boundary involves log h(r1)-log h(r2) and is generally nonlinear; the Gaussian log-prior LDA threshold is not Bayes optimal. This section needs additional distributional or equal-prior restrictions.

Optional after resolving the theorem-level issues: the evidence would be stronger with scaling experiments that directly test support recovery and Bayes-risk convergence, evaluation of the multiclass and QDA algorithms, repeated splits or uncertainty estimates for the small real-data tests, measured runtimes, and released implementation details. Reported model sizes also count transformed coordinates, which are generally dense functions of all raw variables, so they should not be interpreted as raw-feature selection or directly compared with sparse raw-coordinate methods.

The manuscript remains understandable, but numerous notation and exposition errors—such as interchanging Assumption and Condition, confusing d and s, duplicated training-set notation, and unsupported statements about retaining all strong signals—make the technical claims harder to verify and should be corrected.

Theorem 3 asserts almost-sure convergence under log(p)=o(n), whereas its proof concludes only convergence in probability and explicitly invokes log(n)log(p)=o(n), which is strictly stronger. This claim needs substantially narrower distributional/prior assumptions or a different decision rule.

strengths: The core proposal—estimating a symmetric whitening transform under a spiked covariance model, screening the whitened mean difference, and then applying LDA—is coherent and potentially useful to researchers in high-dimensional classification. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/tmlr_2025plus--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-6nahp7i5/call-a9e650e1cb4a4319ae2d538ec0b880ab/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The entrywise eigenspace-perturbation perspective is technically interesting and appropriately targets ℓ∞ estimation and support recovery rather than unnecessarily estimating the entire covariance matrix in spectral norm.

The numerical section includes repeated simulations, multiple covariance structures, several established baselines, oracle comparisons, a sensitivity experiment, and two real gene-expression datasets. The proposed method is often empirically competitive.
The manuscript is generally well organized: assumptions, algorithms, and the distinction between sparsity in raw and whitened coordinates are presented sufficiently clearly for the intended audience.
weaknesses: Necessary: The QDA extension is incorrect. Equation (5.5) is not equivalent to the full QDA rule: sparsity of Wiμi does not make covariance-dependent quadratic terms outside A0 vanish. For example, with u=p^(-1/2)1, Σ1=puuᵀ+I, Σ2=puuᵀ+4I, and means proportional to e1−e2, A0 is fixed and sparse, but the omitted p−2 coordinates contain covariance signal that drives the Bayes error toward zero. Theorem 6 proves only consistency for the restricted score, not equivalence to the Bayes score. The QDA claims must be removed or replaced by substantially stronger assumptions and a new proof.

Necessary: The main LDA consistency result is not established under its stated conditions. Algorithm 1 uses log(n1/n2), but Assumption 3 only requires n1/n2=Θ(1); Equation (8.46) needs n1/n2→π1/(1−π1). Balanced case-control training with unequal population priors is a direct counterexample. Moreover, the proof requires log(n)log(p)=o(n), while the theorem and abstract claim log(p)=o(n), and it concludes convergence in probability after claiming almost-sure convergence of the conditional risk. The abstract's growing-sparsity condition is also not proved because Assumption 2 fixes the support size.

Necessary: The whitening estimator and its proof use inconsistent eigenvalue definitions. The manuscript defines Λ̂ as the top full sample eigenvalues, so (Λ̂+σ̂²I)^(-1/2) double-counts the bulk variance; correspondingly, Equation (8.31) omits a σ²−σ̂² term. These definitions and all dependent bounds need correction.

Necessary: The claimed adaptation to unknown d is unsupported as written. When p≫n, non-spike sample eigenvalues generally scale as p/n rather than O(σ²), so the asserted eigengap Ω(p) is false. The operational experiments instead use an unrelated 90%-explained-variance heuristic, which can retain many noise components and has no stated guarantee.

Necessary: The elliptical-distribution extension overclaims Bayes optimality. With unequal priors and a general monotone radial density h, the likelihood-ratio boundary is not Fisher's Gaussian linear rule; this equivalence requires additional restrictions such as the Gaussian exponential generator, or a substantially narrower setting.

Necessary: The reported oracle simulations are inconsistent with the stated models. Under Model 2 and equal priors, Equation (3.1) gives oracle errors approximately 5.28%, 3.62%, 1.96%, 0.59%, and 0.02% for the five ρ values, whereas Table 3 reports roughly 5.3% throughout. Model 1 at ρ=0.8 should have about 0.022% oracle error, not 0.19%. The experiments therefore require an audit and rerun. Additionally, none of the simulations satisfies all theoretical assumptions simultaneously.

Optional: Representation-size claims should emphasize that a selected whitened coordinate can depend densely on all p raw variables, so these counts are not directly comparable to raw-feature selection and do not reduce measurement requirements. Runtime experiments, scaling studies, complete implementation details, and multiclass/QDA experiments would also strengthen the empirical case.

strengths: The central LDA question is well motivated and relevant to researchers working on high-dimensional classification, factor models, and covariance estimation.

The main technical approach is promising: entrywise eigenspace perturbation bounds are connected to sup-norm estimation of the whitened mean difference, support recovery, and Bayes-risk consistency under a clearly stated spiked-covariance regime.

The algorithms and assumptions are generally presented clearly, and the related-work discussion usefully distinguishes sparsity of the whitened direction from sparsity of the raw discriminant direction.
The empirical section includes 200-replicate simulations, several comparator methods, model-size reporting, a sensitivity experiment, and two real-data examples.
weaknesses: Necessary: The QDA extension is not valid under the stated assumptions. Equation (5.5) replaces the full QDA quadratic forms by norms restricted to A0, the support of the whitened means. When Σ1 differs from Σ2, quadratic terms outside A0 generally do not cancel. Consequently Algorithm 4 is not generally the Bayes rule, and Theorem 6 and the abstract's QDA Bayes-optimality claim are unsupported. This extension must be removed or rebuilt under assumptions controlling the covariance-discriminative directions.

Necessary: The reported oracle simulation results conflict with the stated data-generating models. For Model 2, the specified covariance and mean difference imply Bayes errors of approximately 5.28%, 3.62%, 1.96%, 0.59%, and 0.02% as ρ ranges from 0.5 to 0.9, whereas Table 3 reports roughly 5.2–5.5% throughout. For Model 1 at ρ=0.8, the stated model gives about 0.022%, not the reported 0.19%. The simulations and implementation therefore require an audit and corrected results.

Necessary: The proof of Theorem 3 does not establish its stated almost-sure conclusion under the stated growth condition. It ultimately invokes ln(n)ln(p)=o(n), which is stronger than ln(p)=o(n), and applies Borel–Cantelli to O(p^-2) probabilities without assuming their summability along the asymptotic sequence. The final argument itself only states convergence in probability. The conditions should be strengthened or the conclusion weakened and reproved.

Necessary: The claimed adaptivity is not aligned with the analyzed procedure. The theory uses a prescribed hard threshold and a factor-count estimator based on a diverging eigenvalue ratio, while Algorithm 1 and the experiments use cross-validated top-s selection and a 90%-explained-variance rule. The latter can select a growing number of components even under the theoretical model and has no supplied guarantee. Claims connecting theory to the implemented classifier should be narrowed or tuning consistency established.

Necessary: The elliptical-distribution extension is too broad. For a general monotone radial density and unequal class priors, the Bayes likelihood-ratio boundary is not the Gaussian LDA boundary; sub-Gaussian tails alone do not change this. The result needs additional distributional/prior assumptions or should target the optimal linear rule rather than unrestricted Bayes risk.

Optional: The computational-advantage claim lacks runtime or scaling experiments, the two real-data evaluations use small fixed test splits, and counts of whitened coordinates are not directly comparable to raw-feature selection because each whitened coordinate can depend on all original variables. These claims would benefit from more careful qualification and reproducibility details.

strengths: The manuscript addresses an identifiable problem of interest: high-dimensional classification when covariance structure is dense but governed by pervasive factors. The distinction between sparsity of the raw discriminant direction and sparsity after symmetric whitening is useful. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/tmlr_2025plus--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-bd8hx5xz/call-a023764ae2d84562809cb3f100ef7e00/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The entrywise eigenspace-perturbation approach is technically relevant: uniform control of the estimated whitened direction is the appropriate type of result for subsequent coordinate screening.
The method is conceptually simple, and the paper clearly relates it to sparse LDA, independence rules, factor models, and earlier PCA-based classifiers.

The simulations cover several correlation structures and show substantial finite-sample gains in some settings; the real-data results also suggest competitive prediction using few transformed coordinates. The presentation is generally organized and readable.
weaknesses: Necessary: the QDA extension is mathematically invalid as stated. Equation (5.5) is not a rewrite of the Bayes rule in (5.3): outside A0, the term sum over j not in A0 of [(W1(Z−μ1))j²−(W2(Z−μ2))j²] generally remains when Σ1 differs from Σ2. Sparsity of Wiμi does not eliminate covariance information. For example, unequal bulk variances can make the Bayes error tend to zero using all p coordinates while Algorithm 4 retains only a fixed-dimensional mean-support set. Consequently, Algorithm 4 and Theorem 6 require fundamentally stronger covariance-support assumptions or should be removed.

Necessary: Theorem 3 claims almost-sure Bayes consistency under log p=o(n), but its proof obtains a score bound requiring log n·log p=o(n). It also invokes Borel–Cantelli from an O(p^−2) failure probability without assuming that the sequence sum p_n^−2 is finite, and finishes with convergence in probability of a random score rather than establishing almost-sure convergence of the conditional risk. The theorem and inherited multiclass result therefore are not proved under their stated conditions.

Necessary: the definition of the whitening estimator is inconsistent with its proof. Section 2 defines hatΛ as the leading sample eigenvalues and then uses hatD=(hatΛ+hatσ²I)^−1/2, even though those sample eigenvalues already estimate λk+σ². Equation (8.31), however, treats hatΛ+hatσ² as the sample eigenspectrum. The displayed equality with Uᵀ(Σ−hatΣ)hatU is false under the stated definition. The estimator used experimentally must be clarified and the bounds rederived.

Necessary: the abstract's growing-sparsity condition s·sqrt(log p/n)→0 is unsupported. Assumption 2 fixes s≤M, imposes constant beta-min separation, and bounds the signal norm; Remark 1 explicitly leaves growing s unproved. The headline claim should be narrowed or a complete growing-s analysis supplied.

Necessary: the claimed adaptivity to the unknown number of spikes is not established. In the p/n→∞ regime, the largest non-spike sample eigenvalue is generally of order σ²p/n, not O(σ²) as asserted. Moreover, an Ω(log p) rule is not an operational finite-sample estimator, while the 90%-explained-variance heuristic used experimentally is not covered by the theory and may select many bulk components.

Necessary: the elliptical-distribution extension is too broad. For a general radial density h and unequal class priors, the Bayes boundary compares log h(q1)−log h(q2), which is not generally Fisher's linear rule; Gaussian-type generators or additional restrictions are required.

Optional improvement: none of the principal simulations simultaneously satisfies all central assumptions—Models 1 and 3 have dense whitened directions, while the localized spike in the sensitivity experiment violates bounded coherence. Scaling experiments in the actual theoretical regime, plus experiments for QDA, multiclass, and elliptical claims, would make the evidence much more convincing.

Optional improvement: counts of selected whitened coordinates are not directly comparable to counts of selected raw variables because each whitened coordinate can depend on every original input. This distinction should be emphasized, and runtime experiments and reproducible code should support the claimed computational advantage.

strengths: The manuscript addresses an identifiable audience interested in high-dimensional classification and factor/spiked-covariance models. The central idea—estimate a symmetric whitening transform using principal components, screen the whitened mean difference, and then apply LDA—is intuitive and potentially useful. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/tmlr_2025plus--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-lqx1mess/call-9054d2433af646d69670e17f8ad72278/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The equal-covariance Gaussian analysis explicitly states its structural assumptions and develops entrywise eigenspace, whitening-direction, support-recovery, and classification-risk results. Using two-to-infinity perturbation bounds is technically relevant to coordinate screening.

The empirical section covers several covariance structures, reports variability over 200 Monte Carlo replications, compares against multiple established classifiers, and includes two real gene-expression datasets.

The exposition is generally well organized, with explicit algorithms and useful discussion of how the method differs from sparse-discriminant-direction estimators. The authors also acknowledge that some simulations lie outside the sparse theoretical regime and that the exact spiked model is restrictive.
weaknesses: Necessary: The advertised QDA extension is mathematically invalid. Equation (5.5) drops every coordinate outside the support of the whitened class means, but covariance differences in those coordinates remain discriminative. Even if ζ1 and ζ2 are supported only on coordinate 1, differing Σ1 and Σ2 can carry substantial class information through all other coordinates. Theorem 6 therefore establishes, at most, estimation of a truncated score—not convergence to the Bayes QDA rule. This claim must be withdrawn or replaced by substantially stronger structural assumptions and a new proof.

Necessary: The elliptical-distribution extension incorrectly asserts that Fisher's linear rule is Bayes-optimal for general common-shape elliptical densities. With unequal priors and a non-Gaussian radial density h, the likelihood-ratio boundary is generally nonlinear; monotonicity of h is insufficient. The result needs restriction, such as equal priors or the Gaussian radial form, or a derivation for the actual Bayes rule.

Necessary: The main LDA consistency theorem is false under its stated sampling assumptions. Assumption 3 only requires n1/n2=Θ(1), yet the proof asserts that log(n1/n2) converges to the population log-prior odds. This requires labeled observations sampled from the mixture, or an explicit condition n1/n2→π1/(1−π1); fixed case-control sample sizes do not provide it. The proof also invokes log(n)log(p)=o(n), stronger than the stated log(p)=o(n), and proves joint convergence in probability without establishing the claimed almost-sure convergence of conditional risk.

Necessary: The abstract's growing-sparsity condition is unsupported. The formal analysis assumes a fixed support bounded by M, a fixed beta-min constant, and bounded ‖ζ‖; these conditions themselves preclude growing sparsity. The manuscript explicitly leaves that extension to the reader, so the abstract and conclusions must be narrowed or a complete growing-s proof supplied.

Necessary: The whitening estimator is internally inconsistent. The manuscript defines Λ-hat as the leading sample covariance eigenvalues and then uses (Λ-hat+σ-hat²I)^−1/2, which double-counts the bulk variance; alternatively, Λ-hat would need to denote estimated excess spikes. The algebra around (8.31) likewise omits the corresponding σ²−σ-hat² term. The estimator, implementation, and proof must use one consistent definition. The claim that non-spiked sample eigenvalues are O(σ²) is also false when p/n diverges.

Necessary: Several empirical statements require an audit. Under Model 1 with p=800, ten unit mean shifts, equal priors, and ρ=0.8, the specified model gives squared Mahalanobis separation about 49.375 and Bayes error about 0.022%, not the reported 0.19%; the latter duplicates the ρ=0.7 result. The claim that the proposed method has the highest accuracy is contradicted by Table 1 at ρ=0.8 and 0.9, and the regularized AdaLDA results in Table 5 worsen rather than increase accuracy. These discrepancies call for rerunning and validating the experiments.

Necessary: The practical choice of d as the number of components explaining 90% of variance is not the theoretically discussed spike-count estimator and need not remain fixed under the assumed model. In Model 1 it can retain many bulk sample components. The single sensitivity comparison d=2 versus d=3 does not justify the general claim that overestimation is harmless; selected d values and results for a theoretically justified estimator should be reported.

The parsimony comparison is potentially misleading: one selected whitened coordinate is generally a dense linear combination of all original variables, whereas competing model sizes count selected raw variables. Thus the method does not reduce required measurements or necessarily have fewer stored coefficients. Runtime claims are also unsupported by timing experiments and depend strongly on d. These claims should distinguish transformed dimension from raw-feature sparsity and account for whitening costs.

Optional after correcting the validity issues: evaluate the multiclass, QDA, and elliptical variants empirically; use repeated or nested resampling on more real datasets; report uncertainty for paired method differences, runtimes, seeds, and code. The current two small fixed test sets cannot by themselves support broad claims of state-of-the-art competitiveness.

strengths: The paper studies an identifiable and useful problem: high-dimensional classification under strong-factor/spiked covariance structure. Combining symmetric whitening, screening in the whitened coordinates, and LDA is conceptually interesting and relevant to researchers in high-dimensional statistics. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/tmlr_2025plus--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-xewwv938/call-010e4b02c1ea4f3789673b1041aacd7a/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The main technical strategy is promising: two-to-infinity eigenspace perturbation bounds are used to obtain coordinatewise control of the estimated whitening direction, which naturally supports screening and support-recovery results under explicit strong-spike, incoherence, and sparsity assumptions.

The manuscript is generally well organized, with explicit algorithms, assumptions, and proofs. It also distinguishes sparsity in raw discriminant coordinates from sparsity after whitening, an informative distinction for the intended audience.

The empirical section covers several covariance structures, multiple sparse-classification baselines, a sensitivity experiment, and two gene-expression datasets; within the reported experiments, the proposed method is often accurate while retaining few transformed coordinates.
weaknesses: Necessary: The QDA extension is mathematically invalid as written. Equation (5.5) drops every coordinate outside A0, although A0 is defined only from the supports of W1μ1 and W2μ2. When Σ1 differs from Σ2, the omitted coordinates generally contribute to the quadratic covariance-discrimination term. For example, differing bulk variances can provide information across O(p) coordinates even when both whitened means have fixed sparse support. Thus Equation (5.5) is not equivalent to Bayes QDA, and Theorem 6 and the abstract's QDA Bayes-optimality claim do not follow. This extension needs a new structural assumption and proof, or it should be removed.

Necessary: The main LDA Bayes-consistency theorem lacks a required prior-sampling assumption. Algorithm 1 uses log(n1/n2), while the Bayes rule uses log(π1/(1−π1)); Assumption 3 only requires n1/n2=Θ(1). The proof invokes the strong law to equate these quantities, but the stated class-conditional sampling setup treats n1 and n2 as given and does not ensure convergence to the target population prior. Balanced case-control training with π1≠1/2 is an immediate counterexample. Moreover, Theorem 3 claims almost-sure risk convergence, whereas its proof concludes only convergence in probability of a random score and additionally uses log(n)log(p)=o(n), which is not implied by the stated log(p)=o(n).

Necessary: The whitening estimator is internally inconsistent. The manuscript defines hatΛ as the largest sample covariance eigenvalues but then uses (hatΛ+hatσ²I)^−1/2, thereby adding the bulk variance twice. Correspondingly, the algebra supporting Equation (8.31) drops an extra hatσ² term. These definitions and the affected perturbation proof must be corrected and the claimed rate reverified.

Necessary: The claimed adaptation to unknown d is unsupported in the stated p≫n regime. The manuscript asserts that nonleading sample eigenvalues are O(σ²) and that the relevant eigenvalue ratio is Ω(p); for isotropic noise with p/n→∞, nonzero sample eigenvalues instead scale on the order of p/n. The practical 90%-explained-variance rule is also different from the theoretical ratio rule and can retain many bulk components when the true spikes explain less than 90% of total variance.

Necessary: Some simulation results contradict the analytically known oracle error under the described data-generating models. For Model 2, Equation (3.1) gives oracle errors of approximately 5.28%, 3.62%, 1.96%, 0.59%, and 0.02% as ρ runs from 0.5 to 0.9, but Table 3 reports roughly 5.3% throughout. In Table 1, the reported ρ=0.8 oracle result exactly repeats the ρ=0.7 result, although the corresponding analytic errors are about 0.022% and 0.206%. Several method/model-size entries are duplicated across those columns as well. The simulations therefore require a code and table audit, rerunning, and reproducibility materials before they can support the empirical claims.

Necessary: The elliptical-distribution Bayes-optimality claim is too broad. With a common non-Gaussian radial density h and unequal priors, Bayes classification compares log h(q1)−log h(q2) with the log prior ratio; this is not generally the linear Fisher rule in Equation (1.1). The claim is valid under additional restrictions such as Gaussian h, or equal priors with a common decreasing radial generator, but not for the stated general sub-Gaussian elliptical class.

Optional: The computational-advantage claim is supported only by coarse complexity expressions, not timing or memory measurements. The real-data evidence consists of two small fixed test sets without uncertainty or repeated resampling, and selected whitened coordinates are dense transformations that still require all raw variables. Runtime experiments, stronger validation, and clearer wording around transformed dimension versus raw-feature selection would improve the practical evidence. The manuscript would also benefit from careful proofreading of numerous notation and grammar errors.
